items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 1 with an opening that draws school newspaper readers in by linking the forgotten field to a place they know, while keeping the focus on the marsh. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If you have ever cut through the Brambleton cul-de-sacs on your way to school, you have walked past a field of cattails and cracked pipe that few of us have noticed.
options.label: correct
options.why: Speaks directly to student readers through a familiar route and still sets up the field that sentence 2 identifies as the marsh.

options.text: Since the beginning of human history, people have drained wetlands for farms and towns, and they have often come to regret the choices they made.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: A sweeping historical claim that loses the local, familiar hook and the specific field.

options.text: Finch Lane residents still remember the two days of rain last April, when water crept up to their doorsteps and their basements had to be pumped out.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Moves the flooding evidence in sentence 6 to the start, so the field that sentence 2 calls Cutler's Marsh is never introduced.

options.text: Honestly, most of us could not care less about some swampy old field behind a subdivision, but maybe we should start caring about it a little.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Too casual and dismissive for a paper read by parents and teachers, and it never names the place.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that addresses parents who may worry about the cost of the project to taxpayers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: At that rate, the 180,000-dollar restoration would cost about as much as three floods like last April's, and the town would not have to pay it again.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses the figures from sentences 4 and 6 to answer a cost worry with a comparison taxpayers can follow.

options.text: Parents should stop worrying about money, because protecting nature is always worth whatever it ends up costing the town and its taxpayers.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Brushes off the audience's concern instead of answering it, and the claim is not supported.

options.text: The water on Finch Lane was muddy and cold, and several families had to move furniture to the upper floors of their homes that weekend.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds vivid detail about the flood but says nothing about cost to taxpayers.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would also save the town money on mowing, road salt and school supplies for many decades after the project is done.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Claims savings that nothing in the draft backs up, and school supplies have nothing to do with the project.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that takes a clear position and previews the three benefits discussed in the rest of the editorial. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, because it would ease flooding, keep mosquitoes in check and give our biology classes an outdoor lab.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews flooding, mosquitoes and the lab, in the order the paragraphs follow.

options.text: Cutler's Marsh was once home to many plants and animals, and people in Larkfield have had different opinions about its future over time.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: States no position and previews none of the editorial's points.

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, mainly because doing so would finally put an end to the flooding on Finch Lane.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Takes a position but previews only flooding, leaving out mosquitoes and the lab.

options.text: Although restoring Cutler's Marsh would ease flooding, the costs and the mosquitoes mean the town council should think twice about it.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Argues against the plan the editorial supports.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the sponge comparison connects to the flooding described in sentence 6. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Had the marsh been holding water last April, much of that rain would have soaked into it slowly instead of rushing toward Finch Lane.
options.label: correct
options.why: Applies the sponge comparison to the April flood, linking the evidence to the claim.

options.text: Sponges are simple sea animals, and some kinds can soak up many times their own weight in water before they release it.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Picks up the word sponge but drifts to biology facts with no link to the flood.

options.text: Many other towns have restored marshes over the years, and residents there are often quite proud of the work they did.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Changes the subject to other towns instead of explaining the connection.

options.text: The ditches dug forty years ago, though, are the reason the field is so dry and cracked today, as readers may recall.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Looks back to sentence 2's history and never ties the sponge to the April flooding.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a phrase at the beginning of sentence 10 (adjusting capitalization as needed) to show that the outdoor lab is one more benefit added to those already discussed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Beyond controlling floods and mosquitoes,
options.label: correct
options.why: Marks the lab as an extra benefit on top of the earlier two.

options.text: Despite controlling floods and mosquitoes,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals contrast where the writer is adding a benefit.

options.text: As a result of the flooding,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly makes the lab a result of the flooding.

options.text: On the other hand, for students,
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sets up an opposing point instead of one more benefit.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 with a concrete example showing how the marsh would offer hands-on learning that a textbook cannot. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Students could test the water each month and compare the samples before and after storms, seeing for themselves how a wetland filters runoff.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives a specific hands-on activity that a textbook cannot replace.

options.text: Learning is important, and students deserve good opportunities to explore science in many different ways during their years in school.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Too general; it offers no concrete marsh activity.

options.text: Our textbooks already include detailed chapters on wetlands, with clear diagrams of water cycles and many color photos of marsh animals.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Suggests textbooks are already enough, which undercuts the point.

options.text: The marsh could also become a popular spot for families to walk dogs, watch birds and take photos on quiet weekend mornings.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Describes recreation, not learning.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 1 and 2 clearly and concisely, keeping both the field's location and the fact that it was once a marsh. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field of cattails that was, forty years ago, Cutler's Marsh, until a developer drained it for houses never built.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the location, the history and the cause in one clear, concise sentence.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field, it was Cutler's Marsh forty years ago, until a developer drained it for houses that were never built.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A comma splice joins two independent clauses.

options.text: A developer forty years ago drained a field for houses never built that lies behind the Brambleton subdivision and was Cutler's Marsh.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Keeps the facts, but the modifiers are misplaced, so it sounds as if the houses lie behind the subdivision.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision there lies, past the very last cul-de-sac, a field that in the past, about forty years ago, was once Cutler's Marsh.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Wordy and repetitive, and it leaves out the developer's draining.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 7 into two independent clauses: "A marsh works like a sponge" and "it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly." Which choice joins them correctly?

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge; it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge, it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Comma splice.

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Run-on sentence with no punctuation between the clauses.

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge; and it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A semicolon followed by a conjunction is incorrect here.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence at the end of the report, after sentence 15, that closes by reminding the Student Activities Board of the season's concrete results and connecting them to the modest request. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A team that turned a robot that could not turn left into a ninth-place finisher on donated parts has shown what a small investment can return.
options.label: correct
options.why: Recalls specific results from the report (the November failure, ninth place, donated equipment) and ties them to the idea of a small investment, which fits the board's concern with careful spending.

options.text: Robotics is the future, and every school that ignores it will be left behind by the schools that take it seriously.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Moves to a sweeping, unsupported claim about schools in general instead of the Gearhounds' own results.

options.text: Thank you for reading this report, and please feel free to stop by the woodshop if you have any questions at all.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A polite sign-off that mentions no results and does not link them to the funding request.

options.text: Marmalade got its name from the orange zip ties that held most of its wiring together during the whole season.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Repeats a minor detail from sentence 2 and has nothing to do with the request.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 14 so that the appeal rests on values the Student Activities Board holds: participation, learning, and careful use of money. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The board should fund us because steady attendance and new skills came from very little money, and the funding would build on both.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names all three of the board's values (participation, learning, frugality) and links them to the request.

options.text: The board should fund us because robotics is clearly more exciting than the other clubs asking for money this spring.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Keeps the competitive, boastful appeal instead of pointing to the board's values.

options.text: The board should fund us because the team had so much fun this year and would love to keep the good times going.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Hints at enthusiasm, but it says nothing about learning or careful spending.

options.text: The board should fund us because next year we plan to win the whole Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore outright.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a promise the report gives no evidence for, and it ignores the board's values.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 4 so that the introduction tells the board why the report matters to its upcoming decision. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked new clubs for a summary, and these results bear directly on its budget vote.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the exigence and states outright that the report's results bear on the board's vote.

options.text: I am writing it because my adviser said that writing reports is good practice for college applications later on.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Swaps in a personal reason that has nothing to do with the board's decision.

options.text: I am writing it because the board asked, though honestly most of what we did is easier to show than to explain.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Undercuts the report and is too casual for this audience.

options.text: I am writing it because the Student Activities Board, which meets monthly in the library, likes to keep paper records.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Adds a trivial detail about the board instead of linking the report to the vote.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that makes a claim the report must prove and that previews its three body sections: the build, the members' learning, and next year's needs. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: In one season the Gearhounds built a working robot, turned beginners into capable builders, and now need only modest support to continue.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim and previews the build, the learning, and the needs, in the same order as the paragraphs.

options.text: This report describes the Gearhounds' first season, including the robot, the members, and the competition in Dunmore.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Lists topics without making a claim, and it does not preview the funding section.

options.text: Robotics teaches young people engineering, teamwork, and persistence better than almost any other school activity can.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes a claim about robotics in general, not about this team, and does not match the report's structure.

options.text: The Gearhounds placed ninth out of twenty-six teams, which proves the club deserves full funding for many years ahead.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Rests everything on one fact, overstates the conclusion, and previews no structure.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 12 that explains how the attendance record supports the report's claim that the club deserves continued funding. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: That consistency suggests the money would serve a committed group rather than a club that fades once the novelty wears off.
options.label: correct
options.why: Explains what the attendance shows (commitment) and links it to the funding argument by answering the worry that a new club may not last.

options.text: Exam week this year fell in the middle of January, which is earlier than usual for Harlow Creek High School.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds a side detail about the calendar instead of explaining the evidence.

options.text: Ms. Delacroix-Tam also teaches two sections of chemistry and helps supervise the science fair each spring.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves the focus to the adviser's other duties and draws no link to the funding argument.

options.text: Because attendance stayed above nine, the club will certainly grow to more than twenty members next year.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Predicts with certainty something the evidence does not support.

items.stem: In sentence 1, the writer wants to replace "no idea how to build a robot" with wording that admits the team's inexperience in a tone suited to a formal report for a budget committee. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: no prior experience building a robot
options.label: correct
options.why: States the inexperience plainly, in a measured, formal register.

options.text: absolutely zero clue what we were doing
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Slangy and exaggerated, the same kind of casual tone the draft should avoid.

options.text: a total lack of any kind of competence
options.label: reversal
options.why: Turns inexperience into incompetence, which works against the writer's case.

options.text: limited familiarity with engineering ideas
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Sounds formal but plays down the team's starting point and blurs the before-and-after contrast.
